Hole
HOLE
n.
From Anglo-Saxon hol, a hollow place, a cavern. Webster 1828: a hollow place or cavity in any solid body; an opening. Isaiah tells a people to look back at the pit they were dug from, and the reason he gives is comfort.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah addresses people already seeking the LORD and tells them to look backward, not for shame but for encouragement: Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1). The next verse names the rock and the pit — Abraham and Sarah, called when he was one and childless. The argument is that God multiplied from a single barren couple, and will do so again. The word also names a small and homely mechanism of temple reform: Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar (2 Kings 12:9) — the first collection box in Scripture, introduced because money given for repairs had not been reaching the repairs. Isaiah uses the word again for the peace of the coming kingdom, where the deadliest thing in a child’s world is harmless: the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den (Isaiah 11:8). And the Song has the beloved reach through: My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him (Song of Solomon 5:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HOLE as a hollow place or cavity in any solid body; an opening or perforation; a cave or den; a mean habitation.

expand to see more

HOLE, n. — A hollow place or cavity in any solid body, of any shape or dimensions.

An opening or perforation; as a hole in a garment.

A cave; a den; a hollow place in the earth; the retreat of a beast.

A mean habitation; a narrow or dark lodging.

Anglo-Saxon hol, a hollow; connected with hollow and hell in its older sense of a covered place.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 51:1 — "Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged."

2 Kings 12:9 — "But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one cometh into the house of the LORD: and the priests that kept the door put therein all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD."

Isaiah 11:8 — "And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den."

Isaiah 51:2 — "Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 51:1-2 tells believers to remember what they were dug from, and the remembering is offered as comfort rather than as shame — an order the therapeutic and the moralistic both get wrong.

expand to see more

Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged — and the next verse identifies them: Abraham, called alone, and Sarah, who bore. The recollection is meant to encourage a small and discouraged remnant by reminding them that God has built a nation out of less than they currently have. Two habits get this wrong. The moralistic use makes the pit a rebuke, a reminder of unworthiness deployed to keep a believer humbled; Isaiah uses it to raise their hopes. The therapeutic instinct avoids the pit altogether, on the ground that dwelling on origins is unhelpful; Isaiah commands the looking. Paul does the same in 1 Corinthians 6:11 — such were some of you — and in Ephesians 2:11-13, where remembering what they were is the ground of wonder at what they are.

2 Kings 12:9 is an unexpectedly practical text. Money given for the repair of the house of the LORD had been collected for years and the breaches were not being mended, so Jehoiada bored a hole in a chest lid and set it by the altar, and 2 Kings 12:15 records that no reckoning was required of the men who handled it, for they dealt faithfully. Both halves are instructive: the structure was changed so that giving reached its object, and the men who then handled it were trustworthy enough that auditing was unnecessary. Scripture’s pattern for church finance is neither naive nor suspicious — Paul arranged for the collection to be carried by chosen representatives, providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (2 Corinthians 8:21).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maqqebeth (H4718), a hole or excavation; chor (H2356), a hole or cavity; bor (H953), a pit or cistern; gur (H4631), a den.

expand to see more

Hebrew maqqebeth (H4718) — an excavation or quarry-hole; the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1).

Hebrew bor (H953) — a pit, well or cistern, often hewn from rock; the pit of the same verse.

Hebrew chor (H2356) — a hole or aperture; the hole of the asp (Isaiah 11:8) and the hole of the door (Song of Solomon 5:4).

Hebrew naqab (H5344) — to bore or pierce; Jehoiada boring the chest lid (2 Kings 12:9).

Hebrew pethen (H6620) — the asp or cobra; the creature made harmless in Isaiah 11:8.

Usage

"Look... to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1) — the remembering is comfort, not rebuke."

"Bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar (2 Kings 12:9) — the first collection box, and the reason it was needed."

"The sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp (Isaiah 11:8) — the deadliest thing in a child’s world made harmless."
